title: St Justin Martyr and the charge of subordinationism
subtitle: Order and origin in God are not inequality of nature.
summary: St Justin writes more than a century and a half before Nicaea, in words the Church had not yet fixed. He calls the Son "another God and Lord subject to the Maker of all things" and gives him "the second place". He also worships him, calls him God, and denies that the Father's essence is divided in begetting him. Everything turns on the difference between order and causal origin, what the Greek Fathers call taxis, and inferiority of nature. Drawn from the Dialogue with Trypho, the two Apologies, and Basil the Great on number and nature.

essay.text: A believer who reads about the Fathers online will meet the claim early and often: that the faith of Nicaea was invented in the fourth century, and that the Christians of the second century believed something else. St Justin Martyr is usually the first witness called, because he is the first Christian writer who tries at length to say how the Son stands to the Father, and because he says it in words the Church had not yet fixed. The question is not only for scholars. If the Church changed her faith once, she can change it again, and nothing she confesses is safe. So it is worth taking the hardest sentences in Justin slowly, quoting them whole, and asking what he is actually claiming.

Two very different claims travel under one word. The first is that the Son is from the Father as from his source, that the Father alone is unbegotten, and that there is an order in God, what the Greek Fathers call taxis, in which the Father is the principle and the cause. This the Orthodox Church confesses to this day and calls the monarchy of the Father. The second claim is that the Son is less than the Father in what he is, a lower grade of divinity, a being made rather than begotten. That is Arianism, and the Church condemned it. Any honest reading of Justin has to decide which of the two he is saying, and the way to decide is to let him finish his sentences.
The sentences that sound like inequality

There is no reason to hide them. In the Dialogue with Trypho, Justin undertakes to prove "that there is, and that there is said to be, another God and Lord subject to the Maker of all things." In the First Apology, presenting the faith to an emperor, he says that Christians worship Christ "having learned that He is the Son of the true God Himself, and holding Him in the second place, and the prophetic Spirit in the third." In the Second Apology he writes that "next to God, we worship and love the Word." A reader who stops there has grounds for the charge. A reader who continues finds Justin qualifying his own language within a few lines. The Son, he says, is distinct from the Maker of all things "numerically, I mean, not [distinct] in will," and has never at any time done anything the Father did not will. He is called an Angel, Justin explains more than once, not because he belongs among the angels but "because He announces to men" whatever the Father wishes announced, and "because He ministered to His will." The word is a name of office. The above and the below in these passages concern who appears in the world and who remains unseen, not who is greater.

Justin's own analogy for the begetting says more than any of his titles. When we speak a word, he says, we beget the word, "yet not by abscission, so as to lessen the word [which remains] in us"; and when one fire kindles another, the first is "not lessened when it has kindled [another], but remains the same," while the second "appears to exist by itself, not diminishing that from which it was kindled." He returns to the image near the end of the Dialogue and makes it exact: the Son was begotten "by His power and will, but not by abscission, as if the essence of the Father were divided." This is the picture the Council of Nicaea will take up when it confesses Light of Light, and Justin uses it for the same purpose, to deny that anything in God is cut, spent, or parcelled out. A man who thought the Logos a lesser being would have no reason to labour the point that the Father loses nothing. And when Justin states the relation directly, he states it as origin: the Father is "the cause of His power and of His being Lord and God." Cause is not rank. It says where the Son is from.
The Church at prayer answers first

The surest test of what a second-century Christian believed about Christ is not his vocabulary but his worship, because a Jew turned philosopher does not offer worship to a creature. Justin offers it, in public, in a document addressed to the Roman state. Father, Son, and prophetic Spirit, he writes, "we worship and adore." The Word "who is from the unbegotten and ineffable God" is worshipped and loved. The Son, "being the first-begotten Word of God, is even God." The Father alone is unbegotten and beyond naming, while the Son "alone is properly called Son." And Justin did not argue this and then walk away from it. He was put to death in Rome under the prefect Rusticus for refusing to sacrifice, and the Church numbers him among the martyrs. What a man dies confessing is the best commentary on what his sentences meant.
What Justin had not yet been given words for

None of this makes Justin a fourth-century theologian, and the Church has never needed him to be one. He has no fixed distinction between essence and person, no settled term for what the Three share and what distinguishes them, no homoousios. He arranges Father, Son, and Spirit in a sequence and leaves the sequence unexplained. In one sentence, on the most natural reading of the English, he lets the good angels stand inside a clause about worship where the Church's later language would not place them, and readers have argued over that clause ever since. These are the marks of a man working before the vocabulary existed, not the marks of a different faith. St Basil the Great, writing more than two centuries afterwards against those who wanted to number the Spirit beneath the Son, gives the rule that settles the matter: "what thing ever lost its own nature by being numbered?" Things counted remain what they were. Order in God is real, the Father is genuinely the source and the cause, and neither of those truths makes the Son or the Spirit less than God. Justin was feeling for that sentence. He did not yet have it. The Church, in her own time and through her councils, wrote it down for him, and in doing so she was not correcting his faith but naming it.

florilegium.author: St Justin Martyr
florilegium.text: I shall attempt to persuade you, since you have understood the Scriptures, [of the truth] of what I say, that there is, and that there is said to be, another God and Lord subject to the Maker of all things; who is also called an Angel, because He announces to men whatsoever the Maker of all things, above whom there is no other God, wishes to announce to them.
florilegium.gloss: The hardest sentence in Justin, quoted without softening. Note that in the same breath he explains what Angel means: it is a name of office, given because the Son announces the Father's will.

florilegium.author: St Justin Martyr
florilegium.text: He who is said to have appeared to Abraham, and to Jacob, and to Moses, and who is called God, is distinct from Him who made all things, numerically, I mean, not [distinct] in will. For I affirm that He has never at any time done anything which He who made the world, above whom there is no other God, has not wished Him both to do and to engage Himself with.
florilegium.gloss: Justin's own qualifier, a few lines later. What he is defending is a distinction of number, of who is who, not a difference of will and not a lower rank in willing.

florilegium.author: St Justin Martyr
florilegium.text: God begot before all creatures a Beginning, [who was] a certain rational power [proceeding] from Himself, who is called by the Holy Spirit, now the Glory of the Lord, now the Son, again Wisdom, again an Angel, then God, and then Lord and Logos; and on another occasion He calls Himself Captain, when He appeared in human form to Joshua the son of Nave (Nun). For He can be called by all those names, since He ministers to the Father's will, and since He was begotten of the Father by an act of will; just as we see happening among ourselves: for when we give out some word, we beget the word; yet not by abscission, so as to lessen the word [which remains] in us, when we give it out: and just as we see also happening in the case of a fire, which is not lessened when it has kindled [another], but remains the same; and that which has been kindled by it likewise appears to exist by itself, not diminishing that from which it was kindled.
florilegium.gloss: The analogy Nicaea will inherit as Light of Light. Its whole force is that nothing in the Father is divided, spent, or lessened by the begetting, which is a strange thing to insist upon if the Begotten were a lesser being.

florilegium.author: St Justin Martyr
florilegium.text: And that this power which the prophetic word calls God, as has been also amply demonstrated, and Angel, is not numbered [as different] in name only like the light of the sun but is indeed something numerically distinct, I have discussed briefly in what has gone before; when I asserted that this power was begotten from the Father, by His power and will, but not by abscission, as if the essence of the Father were divided; as all other things partitioned and divided are not the same after as before they were divided: and, for the sake of example, I took the case of fires kindled from a fire, which we see to be distinct from it, and yet that from which many can be kindled is by no means made less, but remains the same.
florilegium.gloss: Justin is fighting on two fronts at once. Against a modalist reading of the theophanies he insists the Son is really distinct. Against a ditheist reading he insists that nothing is divided: the essence of the Father is not cut.

florilegium.author: St Justin Martyr
florilegium.text: When Scripture says, 'The Lord rained fire from the Lord out of heaven,' the prophetic word indicates that there were two in number: One upon the earth, who, it says, descended to behold the cry of Sodom; Another in heaven, who also is Lord of the Lord on earth, as He is Father and God; the cause of His power and of His being Lord and God.
florilegium.gloss: The whole question in one clause. The Father is the cause of the Son's being Lord and God. Cause is not superiority of nature, it is origin, and the Church confesses it still: from the Father, the one principle, the Son is begotten and the Spirit proceeds.

florilegium.author: St Justin Martyr
florilegium.text: Therefore neither Abraham, nor Isaac, nor Jacob, nor any other man, saw the Father and ineffable Lord of all, and also of Christ, but [saw] Him who was according to His will His Son, being God, and the Angel because He ministered to His will; whom also it pleased Him to be born man by the Virgin; who also was fire when He conversed with Moses from the bush.
florilegium.gloss: Angel is explained again, and the explanation is a work, not a rank of being: because He ministered to His will. The above and below in Justin concern who is seen and who is not.

florilegium.author: St Justin Martyr
florilegium.text: For if you had understood what has been written by the prophets, you would not have denied that He was God, Son of the only, unbegotten, unutterable God.
florilegium.gloss: The plain confession. The Son is God, and the Father alone is unbegotten. Unbegottenness is the Father's personal property, not a higher grade of divinity.

florilegium.author: St Justin Martyr
florilegium.text: Our teacher of these things is Jesus Christ, who also was born for this purpose, and was crucified under Pontius Pilate, procurator of Judæa, in the times of Tiberius Cæsar; and that we reasonably worship Him, having learned that He is the Son of the true God Himself, and holding Him in the second place, and the prophetic Spirit in the third, we will prove.
florilegium.gloss: The text most often produced as proof of subordinationism, quoted whole. Note what it actually says alongside the second place: the Son of the true God himself, and worship offered to him.

florilegium.author: St Justin Martyr
florilegium.text: But both Him, and the Son (who came forth from Him and taught us these things, and the host of the other good angels who follow and are made like to Him), and the prophetic Spirit, we worship and adore, knowing them in reason and truth, and declaring without grudging to every one who wishes to learn, as we have been taught.
florilegium.gloss: The confession of Christian worship: Father, Son, and prophetic Spirit. The clause about the good angels is one of the genuinely difficult sentences in Justin, and the parenthesis around it is the translators' punctuation rather than Justin's. What the sentence as a whole shows is the Church at prayer, not a ladder of gods.

florilegium.author: St Justin Martyr
florilegium.text: For they who affirm that the Son is the Father, are proved neither to have become acquainted with the Father, nor to know that the Father of the universe has a Son; who also, being the first-begotten Word of God, is even God.
florilegium.gloss: Written to a Roman emperor, in public: the Word is God. Justin's argument in this chapter is against collapsing the Son into the Father, not against confessing his divinity.

florilegium.author: St Justin Martyr
florilegium.text: But to the Father of all, who is unbegotten, there is no name given. For by whatever name He be called, He has as His elder the person who gives Him the name. But these words, Father, and God, and Creator, and Lord, and Master, are not names, but appellations derived from His good deeds and functions. And His Son, who alone is properly called Son, the Word, who also was with Him and was begotten before the works, when at first He created and arranged all things by Him, is called Christ, in reference to His being anointed and God's ordering all things through Him.
florilegium.gloss: The Son alone is properly Son. Justin's Father is the unbegotten and unnameable source, which is exactly what later Orthodoxy will call the monarchy of the Father.

florilegium.author: St Justin Martyr
florilegium.text: For next to God, we worship and love the Word who is from the unbegotten and ineffable God, since also He became man for our sakes, that becoming a partaker of our sufferings, He might also bring us healing.
florilegium.gloss: Another sentence critics quote and then stop. Justin worships the Word. A Jew turned philosopher does not offer worship to a creature, whatever else he is prepared to say.

florilegium.author: St Basil the Great
florilegium.reference: Chapter XVII, §43, NPNF Second Series, vol. 8
florilegium.text: Nay, without exception, what thing ever lost its own nature by being numbered? Is it not the fact that things when numbered remain what they naturally and originally were, while number is adopted among us as a sign indicative of the plurality of subjects?
florilegium.gloss: Two centuries later Basil states the rule that settles the question. Number is a sign of how many, not a measure of what. Order within the Trinity is real and it does not make the Son or the Spirit less God.

scripture.note: The Lord appears to Abraham at the oak of Mamre, the theophany Justin argues over for a dozen chapters of the Dialogue.
The Lord rained fire from the Lord out of heaven, Justin's central proof that Scripture itself names two.
The Angel of the Lord in the bush who then says I AM. Justin reads him as the Son, so that Angel here means messenger, not creature.
Wisdom brought forth before the works, quoted by Justin for the begetting before all creatures and later turned by the Arians to the opposite purpose.
The Word was with God and the Word was God. The distinction and the divinity stand in one verse.
My Father is greater than I, read by the Fathers of the Son's origin from the Father and of his assumed humanity, never of a lesser divinity.

editorialNotes: VERIFICATION RUN, WHAT WAS ACTUALLY CHECKED. This draft was passed through a rights and accuracy gate with live network access on 2026-07-25. All thirteen florilegium entries were fetched from their sources and compared word by word. All thirteen are confirmed present, in the stated translation, attributed to the stated Father, in the stated work, at the stated chapter. Nothing was deleted. Four material corrections were made and are listed below. Sources actually opened: newadvent.org/fathers/01285.htm, 01289.htm, 0126.htm, and ccel.org anf01.viii.ii.lxiii.html, anf01.viii.iii.vi.html, anf01.viii.iii.xiii.html, npnf208.vii.xviii.html.

CORRECTION ONE, ALTERED PATRISTIC WORD, NOW FIXED. The Dialogue 61 entry read 'God begat before all creatures a Beginning'. The Ante-Nicene Fathers text reads 'God begot'. The verb had been changed. It has been restored to 'begot'. This is the single most serious defect found and it is exactly the kind of drift that must never reach a reader. The rest of that entry matches ANF word for word.

CORRECTION TWO, EVERY DIALOGUE URL WAS WRONG. The draft's own notes flagged the Dialogue page assignments as estimates. They were wrong. New Advent splits the Dialogue as follows, confirmed by opening the pages: 01282.htm holds chapters 10 to 30, 01284.htm holds 48 to 54, 01285.htm holds 55 to 68, 01286.htm holds 69 to 88, 01288.htm holds 109 to 124, 01289.htm holds 125 to 142. Chapters 56 and 61 now point to 01285.htm and chapters 126 to 129 now point to 01289.htm. The draft's reasoning rested on an existing app file, and that file is itself wrong: see the note on theosis.json below.

CORRECTION THREE, FACTUAL ERROR IN THE SUMMARY. The summary said Justin writes 'eighty years before Nicaea'. The Dialogue dates to roughly the middle of the second century and Justin died about 165; Nicaea met in 325. The true gap is more than a century and a half, not eighty years. The summary now reads 'more than a century and a half before Nicaea', and the essay's description of Basil has been changed from 'two hundred years afterwards' to 'more than two centuries afterwards', which is the honest figure for a work of 375.

CORRECTION FOUR, DROPPED COMMAS IN SECOND APOLOGY 6. Three commas present in the Ante-Nicene Fathers text had been dropped from that quotation: after 'who is unbegotten', after 'But these words', and after 'the Word'. All three are restored. Small, but a quotation is either exact or it is not.

EM DASHES, HOW THEY WERE HANDLED. The ANF text of Dialogue 56 sets 'above whom there is no other God' between em dashes in two places, and puts an em dash before 'numerically, I mean'. House style forbids em dashes in user-facing copy. The earlier draft rendered the first pair as parentheses; they are now commas, which is the remedy house style names, and the dash before 'numerically' is a comma. No word has been added, removed, reordered, or modernized in any quotation anywhere in this study. If a reviewer wants strict typographic fidelity instead, the two Dialogue 56 excerpts should be re-cut to end before the dashes rather than punctuated around them.

SOURCE HOSTS ARE MIXED, ON PURPOSE. New Advent's single-page files for the First Apology, the Second Apology, and Basil's De Spiritu Sancto are too long to retrieve past roughly chapter 50, chapter 6, and chapter 15 respectively, so First Apology 63, both Second Apology entries, and the Basil entry could not be confirmed there and are cited to the Christian Classics Ethereal Library instead, where they were confirmed. Both hosts carry the same public-domain translations. First Apology 6 and 13 were confirmed on New Advent and keep that URL. If house preference is a single host, move the CCEL entries to New Advent only after someone opens the New Advent page in a browser and reads the chapter, not by pattern-matching a URL.

PRE-EXISTING BUG IN SHIPPED CONTENT. data/theology/theosis.json cites Dialogue with Trypho 124 to https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/01284.htm. That page holds chapters 48 to 54. Dialogue 124 is on 01288.htm. This is already live and should be fixed independently of this study. data/theology/the-theotokos.json cites Dialogue 100 to 01287.htm, which is the correct page for chapters 89 to 108.

DATA BUG IN THE APP'S OWN JUSTIN TEXT, CONFIRMED BY INSPECTION. data/saints/justin-martyr/dialogue-with-trypho.json was read directly. The file has 142 sections but its numbering slips: section n=60 contains both ANF chapter 60 and ANF chapter 61, with the ANF running header 'Wisdom is begotten of the Father, as fire from fire' surviving as a stray line inside it and the fire-from-fire text sitting there. Section n=61 carries the title of true ANF chapter 62, and n=114 carries the title of true ANF chapter 115. Numbering re-syncs by n=126. This study cites TRUE ANF chapter numbers, so a reader tapping through from the Dialogue 61 citation will land on the wrong in-app chapter. Fix before or alongside shipping.

COPYRIGHT SUBSTITUTION, PLEASE SANITY-CHECK THE ARGUMENT. The Discord thread quotes the Thomas B. Falls translation (Fathers of the Church, 1948), which is under copyright and is not used here. Where the thread quoted Falls, the ANF wording has been substituted. The most consequential difference is at Dialogue 56: Falls reads 'another God and Lord under the Creator of all things'; ANF reads 'another God and Lord subject to the Maker of all things'. The thread builds a paragraph on the spatial force of the word 'under'. ANF's 'subject to' is, if anything, harder for the argument, and the essay was written to face that rather than lean on 'under'. Confirm the substitution has not quietly changed what is being claimed.

MODERN SCHOLARSHIP ENTRIES WERE REWRITTEN TO REMOVE CLOSE PARAPHRASE. Three entries in the earlier draft tracked their sources' wording too closely: the Bird entry reproduced in substance a sentence Bird himself quotes from Eric Osborn, the White entry echoed his phrasing about proto-Trinitarian and unitarian, and the Olson and Hall entry echoed a phrase about Justin being kept on course. All three are now descriptions of the argument in independent words, with nothing quoted. The Olson and Hall entry now also flags that the thread's excerpt from that book contains a further quotation from Gerald O'Collins, so there is a second layer of copyright behind it. The essay and every gloss were scanned for lifted sentences and none were found; the prose is original throughout.

ORIGEN IS DELIBERATELY ABSENT. The thread cites the Dialogue with Heraclides at length for the heteros theos vocabulary. That text was only recovered in 1941 and has no public-domain English translation, so it cannot be quoted under our rules and it is not in the florilegium. If you want Origen's witness in this study, we need either a licensed quotation or a third-person editorial digest with citation, and the digest route needs your approval on wording.

PHILO IS DELIBERATELY ABSENT. The thread reproduces Greek from Quaestiones in Genesim II.62 and builds the heteros theos versus deuteros theos argument on it. Quaestiones survives principally in Armenian, the Greek fragment quoted could not be verified, and Yonge's public-domain Philo does not carry the Questions on Genesis in the form given. The essay therefore never quotes Philo and never names him. If you want the Second Temple background made explicit, say so and it can be drafted without quotation.

THE GREEK LEXICAL ARGUMENT IS SOFTENED ON PURPOSE, AND NEEDS A READER WITH GREEK. The thread's central lexical claim is that Justin consistently chooses heteros theos and consistently avoids allos theos, and that the choice is doctrinally load-bearing. In Koine that distinction is not always as sharp as the thread needs it to be, and overstating it would be a genuine error in a teaching document. The essay therefore makes no lexical claim at all. If a reviewer with Greek can confirm Justin's usage really is that consistent, the argument can be added and it would strengthen the study considerably.

DOCTRINAL FORMULATION TO CHECK, ONE. The essay states that the monarchy of the Father, that the Father alone is unbegotten and is the principle and cause within the Trinity, is Orthodox doctrine and is what Justin is reaching for. Please confirm the wording does not slide anywhere into making the Son's divinity derivative in nature rather than only in origin. The sentence carrying the most weight is in the fire section: 'Cause is not rank. It says where the Son is from.'

DOCTRINAL FORMULATION TO CHECK, TWO. The closing paragraph concedes that Justin's vocabulary is pre-technical and that he says things a post-Nicene writer would phrase differently, then says the Church 'was not correcting his faith but naming it'. Confirm that this is honest without implying either that Justin taught error or that doctrinal development is invention. This is the single most likely sentence to be quoted out of context.

DIALOGUE 129 IS LOAD-BEARING. The phrase 'the cause of His power and of His being Lord and God' is the strongest single piece of evidence in the study that Justin's ordering is causal rather than qualitative. The wording is confirmed verbatim against New Advent. What still needs a clergy reader is whether this reading of the passage is the standard one and not an over-read of Roberts and Donaldson's English.

THE HARD TEXTS ARE QUOTED UNSOFTENED, BY CHOICE. First Apology 13 ('the second place... the prophetic Spirit in the third') and Second Apology 13 ('next to God, we worship and love the Word') are in the florilegium in full. Omitting them would be worse than including them, because a reader who later finds them elsewhere would rightly conclude the study was hiding something. If you disagree with that pastoral call, they can be moved into the essay body instead.

THE GOOD ANGELS CLAUSE IN FIRST APOLOGY 6 STILL NEEDS YOUR EYES. The entry keeps the parenthesis 'and the host of the other good angels who follow and are made like to Him', confirmed verbatim on two independent hosts. The parenthesis is the translators' punctuation, not Justin's, and there is a long history of reading the clause as attaching to 'taught us these things' rather than to the objects of worship. The earlier draft's gloss asserted that no later Father repeats the clause; that is an unverifiable universal claim and it has been removed. The gloss now says only that the sentence is genuinely difficult and that the punctuation is editorial. The essay sentence about it has likewise been softened to say that this is the natural reading of the English and that readers have argued over it. Please approve this framing or give me yours; I do not want to resolve it by editorial fiat.

THE MARTYRDOM DETAIL IS DELIBERATELY VAGUE. The essay says Justin 'was put to death in Rome under the prefect Rusticus for refusing to sacrifice' and does not specify the manner of death. The Acts of Justin support the prefect and the refusal. If you want the beheading stated, it should be checked against the recension of the Acts we are willing to stand behind.

BASIL IS THE ONLY POST-NICENE VOICE, AND HE IS DOING REAL WORK. The Basil entry is confirmed verbatim at On the Holy Spirit chapter XVII, section 43, in Blomfield Jackson's NPNF translation. It carries the taxis-versus-nature principle explicitly, since Justin himself never states it. Confirm you are comfortable with a fourth-century text supplying the interpretive key for a second-century one, and that the essay makes clear this is the Church's later clarification rather than something read back into Justin. Athanasius on John 14:28 would have been the natural second witness, but the local copy of the Four Discourses has corrupted quotation marks throughout, so no Athanasius quotation was used.

METADATA. Group is trinity, which is a valid group in lib/theology/topics.ts. The three related slugs, filioque, theosis, and the-theotokos, were all confirmed present in topics.ts. estimatedMinutes has been reduced from 22 to 16, which matches the actual length of the essay plus florilegium at ordinary reading speed. Justin exists in the app as saintSlug justin-martyr with all three works, and Basil as basil-the-great with On the Holy Spirit, so deep links should resolve once the Dialogue numbering bug is fixed. Shipping still requires a new entry in lib/theology/topics.ts, which this draft does not include.

POLEMIC. No opponent is named anywhere and no scorecard is kept. Arianism is named as a condemned teaching, which is a statement of what the councils decided, not an attack on any living communion. Nothing in this study touches Oriental Orthodox or other Christian bodies. If you would prefer an explicit, charitable engagement with the Arian or modern unitarian reading by name, that can be added as one further section.

SECOND VERIFICATION PASS, 2026-07-26. THREE FLAGGED ENTRIES, ALL THREE CONFIRMED, NOTHING CHANGED. scripts/verify-florilegium.mjs flagged three entries in this study: Dialogue 56 at 28 of 72 words, First Apology 13 at 36 of 67, and the other Dialogue 56 excerpt at 57 of 69. I re-fetched each cited page with curl and grepped the raw bytes, deliberately not using a summarising fetch tool: newadvent.org/fathers/01285.htm (78,909 bytes) for both Dialogue 56 entries, newadvent.org/fathers/0126.htm (171,707 bytes) for First Apology 13. All three quotations stand on their cited pages word for word, inside their cited chapters. No text was corrected, no source URL was changed, and no entry was deleted, because there was nothing wrong with any of them. The three flags are false positives generated by the checker itself. The other six New Advent entries were re-run at the same time and remain exact (Dialogue 61 at 180 of 180 words, 128 at 136, 129 at 67, 127 at 69, 126 at 28, First Apology 6 at 62). The four CCEL entries were not re-fetched this pass and rest on the 2026-07-25 check.

WHY THE CHECKER FLAGGED THEM, AND THE ONE-LINE FIX. norm() in scripts/verify-florilegium.mjs strips HTML tags, then strips every non-alphanumeric character, but it decodes only two named entities,   and &. Every other entity survives the tag strip and is then turned into a bare word. New Advent sets the Dialogue 56 dashes as — and prints Judaea and Caesar with the ae ligature as æ. So after normalisation the page reads 'all things mdash above whom there is no other god' and 'jud aelig a ... tiberius c aelig sar', while our quotations normalise to 'all things above whom there is no other god' and 'jud a ... tiberius c sar'. The word sequence breaks at exactly those points, which is exactly where the three flags fall: 28 of 72 breaks at the first dash, 57 of 69 breaks at the second, 36 of 67 breaks at the ligature in Judaea. Suggested fix, one line in norm() before the punctuation strip: .replace(/&[a-zA-Z]+;|&#x?[0-9a-fA-F]+;/g, ' '). With that line the three entries match at full length, 69 of 69, 72 of 72, and 67 of 67, and no other entry in this study changes state. I did not edit the script; whether the gate is patched is your call, and until it is, these three will keep reporting red.

FLAGGED ENTRY 1 OF 3, DIALOGUE 56, the 'another God and Lord subject to the Maker of all things' excerpt, 57 of 69. CONFIRMED VERBATIM, KEPT AS IS. New Advent prints, and I read in the raw bytes: 'I shall attempt to persuade you, since you have understood the Scriptures, [of the truth] of what I say, that there is, and that there is said to be, another God and Lord subject to the Maker of all things; who is also called an Angel, because He announces to men whatsoever the Maker of all things— above whom there is no other God —wishes to announce to them.' Our entry is that sentence exactly, including the translators' square brackets, with the two — rendered as commas under the house rule already recorded above. All 69 words contiguous once the entity is decoded. Chapter attribution checked as well: the passage sits under the page's own heading 'Chapter 56. God who appeared to Moses is distinguished from God the Father'.

FLAGGED ENTRY 2 OF 3, DIALOGUE 56, the 'numerically, I mean, not [distinct] in will' excerpt, 28 of 72. CONFIRMED VERBATIM, KEPT AS IS. The page runs continuously from 'He who is said to have appeared to Abraham' through 'to engage Himself with', with — where our text has a comma in two places, before 'numerically, I mean' and around 'above whom there is no other God'. All 72 words contiguous once the entities are decoded, and the passage is inside chapter 56. One thing for the reviewer, unrelated to the flag: the excerpt begins mid-sentence. modernScholarship.usedFor: The source thread leans on it for the claim that readings of Old Testament theophanies distinguishing two divine figures circulated inside Second Temple Judaism, and that the rabbinic condemnation of two powers was a later reaction rather than the original universal standard.
